title: Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training: A Must-Know for Care Home Managers
excerpt: The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on learning disability and autism: what care home managers need to know and how HCC-Temps makes sure staff are trained.
content:
As a care home manager, staying informed about essential training programs like the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training is key to ensuring your residents receive the best care. This mandatory training, focused on improving the care provided to individuals with learning disabilities and autism, is something all health and social care professionals need to be familiar with.

At HCC Temps, we understand the importance of compliance, which is why, as of August 2024, we are ensuring our Healthcare and Hospitality Staff are trained and compliant with this mandatory program. If you’re a care home manager looking to strengthen your team and maintain top-quality care, visit our website to get covered with fully trained and compliant staff.

What is the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training?

The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training ensures that all health and social care staff have the knowledge and skills necessary to provide safe, effective care for people with learning disabilities and autism. This training is mandatory for all staff across care homes, from care assistants and nurses to kitchen and housekeeping teams.
There are two key levels of training:

    • Tier 1: Basic awareness training for all staff, including non-clinical roles.
    • Tier 2: More detailed training for those in clinical or frontline roles who have direct contact with residents with learning disabilities and autism.This tiered approach means that everyone, regardless of their role, will receive the right level of training to support your care home and residents effectively.

Why the Training is Needed: The Story Behind It

The training was named in memory of Oliver McGowan, a young man with learning disabilities and autism who tragically died in 2016 due to inappropriate care. His death highlighted serious gaps in the understanding of healthcare professionals when it came to supporting individuals with conditions around autism.
Oliver’s parents, along with campaigners, fought for mandatory training to prevent similar tragedies in the future. The result is the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training, now a legal requirement for all health and social care staff across the UK. The goal is to bridge the gaps in knowledge and improve outcomes for individuals with learning disabilities and autism.

Why is This Training Important for Care Homes?

As a care home manager, you know that your team’s ability to deliver compassionate, informed care is crucial. People with learning disabilities and autism often face barriers to receiving the care they need due to misunderstandings or a lack of awareness from care staff. This training is designed to address those issues head-on, ensuring that your team is equipped to provide the highest quality care.

Here’s why the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training matters:

    • Improved care quality: Your team will be better prepared to meet the needs of residents with learning disabilities and autism.
    • Compliance with legal requirements: Meeting regulatory standards is essential to avoid penalties and ensure your care home is compliant with national regulations.
    • Promoting dignity and respect: Proper training fosters a culture of dignity, respect, and inclusivity, where all residents are understood and valued.
    • Reducing preventable harm: By enhancing staff knowledge, the risk of preventable incidents and misunderstandings is significantly reduced.

Who Needs to Take the Oliver McGowan Training?

The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training applies to all health and social care staff—no matter their role. Whether you’re managing a team of nurses, care assistants, or support staff, everyone must complete this training. The training is tailored to fit the specific needs of different staff roles, with two levels:

    • Tier 1: Basic training for all staff, including non-clinical roles such as catering and maintenance.
    • Tier 2: Advanced training for clinical and frontline staff who interact directly with residents who have learning disabilities and autism.

By ensuring that all staff are trained, you’re creating a care environment that is safer, more inclusive, and supportive for everyone.

How HCC Temps is Supporting Care Homes: August 2024 and Beyond

At HCC Temps, we are committed to ensuring Oliver’s story is not replicated. As of August 2024 we have begun the ongoing process of ensuring our Healthcare and Hospitality Staff are being trained to meet these mandatory requirements. This means that when you book temporary staff with us, you can be confident that they are fully equipped to provide the best possible care to residents with learning disabilities and autism.

Moving Forward: Embrace Quality Care with HCC Temps

The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training represents an important step forward in making care homes more inclusive, understanding, and supportive for residents with learning disabilities and autism. As a care home manager, ensuring your staff completes this training is a critical part of creating a caring environment where every resident feels safe, respected, and valued.
At HCC Temps, we’re here to support you in this journey. By providing fully trained and compliant temporary staff, we make it easier for you to focus on what really matters—providing exceptional care to your residents. Visit HCC Temps to book our trained staff and ensure your care home remains compliant and delivers the highest standards of care.

title: Understanding NEWS2: Why It Matters and What We’re Doing About It
excerpt: What NEWS2, the National Early Warning Score, means for care home managers, why it matters for spotting deterioration early, and how HCC-Temps prepares its nurses.
content:
As a home manager, you’re already aware of how crucial it is to provide top-notch care for your residents. A big part of that is ensuring your nursing team is up-to-date with the latest tools and training. One key update is the National Early Warning Score, or NEWS2. If you’re not familiar with it yet, don’t worry—we’re here to explain why NEWS2 is important and what we’re doing to make sure our nurses are fully trained and compliant.

What’s NEWS2?

NEWS2 is the latest version of the National Early Warning Score system, used to spot early signs that a resident’s health might be getting worse. It helps nursing staff quickly identify problems by scoring vital signs like blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature. If something seems off, NEWS2 guides the team on what steps to take next.

How Did NEWS2 Come About? 

NEWS2 is an upgrade from the original NEWS system, introduced in 2012. Based on feedback and new research, the updated version came out in 2017. It includes clearer guidelines and a few tweaks to make it easier to use, aiming to improve patient safety and communication among healthcare teams.

Why Is NEWS2 So Important?

  • Early Detection: It helps catch potential issues early, which can be critical in preventing serious health problems.
  • Consistency: It standardises how we monitor and respond to changes in a resident’s condition, ensuring everyone is on the same page.
  • Better Communication: It provides a common language for discussing patient conditions and necessary actions.
  • Safer Care: By improving early detection, it helps keep our residents safer.

Who Needs NEWS2 Training?

Everyone on the nursing team should be familiar with NEWS2:

  • Registered Nurses (RNs): They use NEWS2 to assess and respond to changes in residents’ health.
  • Healthcare Assistants (HCAs): Understanding NEWS2 helps them spot issues early and communicate effectively with RNs.
  • Clinical Managers: They oversee the implementation of NEWS2 and ensure everyone on the team is trained and compliant.

Our Commitment to NEWS2 Compliance

We’re committed to ensuring that all our nursing staff are trained and compliant with NEWS2. Here’s what we’re doing:

  • Training Programs: We offer comprehensive training to cover everything you need to know about NEWS2, from basics to practical application.
  • Ongoing Support: We provide regular updates and refresher courses to keep everyone sharp.
  • Feedback and Improvement: We actively seek feedback to make sure our training is effective and adjust as needed.

title: COSHH: Essential Guidelines for Safe Kitchen Operations
excerpt: COSHH explained for care home kitchens: how to store, use and record hazardous cleaning substances safely and keep kitchen staff and residents protected.
content:
The Control of Substances Hazardous to Health (COSHH) regulations are crucial for maintaining a safe kitchen environment in care homes. These regulations ensure that kitchen staff handle hazardous substances properly to prevent accidents and health issues. Here’s what you need to know to comply with COSHH standards:

Understanding COSHH
COSHH covers any substances that can cause harm if they are not handled correctly. This includes cleaning chemicals, disinfectants, and any other substances used in the kitchen that might pose a risk to health. The primary aim of COSHH is to minimise exposure to these substances through proper management and training.

Storage and Labelling
One of the first steps in COSHH compliance is the proper storage of hazardous substances. Keep cleaning chemicals and other hazardous materials in designated, well-ventilated areas away from food preparation zones. Use clearly labelled containers and ensure that all substances are stored according to the manufacturer’s instructions. This helps prevent accidental exposure and contamination.

Training and Safety Data Sheets (SDS)
All kitchen staff must be trained in COSHH procedures. This training should cover the proper use of hazardous substances, including how to handle spills and emergencies. Staff should also be familiar with Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for each substance used in the kitchen. SDS provides detailed information on the risks associated with each substance, safe handling procedures, and first aid measures.

Handling and Disposal
Proper handling of hazardous substances involves using them according to the manufacturer’s guidelines. Staff should wear appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves and goggles when handling chemicals. Additionally, establish procedures for the safe disposal of hazardous substances, ensuring they are disposed of in accordance with local regulations.

Emergency Procedures
In case of accidental spills or exposure, it’s crucial to have emergency procedures in place. This includes having spill kits readily available and ensuring all staff know how to use them. Regularly review and practise emergency response procedures to keep staff prepared for any incidents involving hazardous substances.

Regular Reviews and Audits
To maintain COSHH compliance, regularly review your practices and conduct audits. This helps identify any gaps in procedures or training and ensures that safety measures are up-to-date. Regular reviews also help in maintaining a safe working environment and in compliance with legal requirements.

By adhering to COSHH regulations, you can create a safer working environment for your kitchen staff and ensure that hazardous substances are managed properly

title: Have You Put Your Enhanced DBS Certificate on the Update Service?
excerpt: Why care workers should register a new enhanced DBS certificate on the DBS Update Service within 30 days, and how it speeds up starting work with an agency.
content:
When you’re working in health and social care, having the right safeguarding checks in place isn’t just a formality – it’s a legal and ethical responsibility. One of the most important checks you’ll need is an Enhanced DBS (Disclosure and Barring Service) certificate.

But here’s a point that many candidates overlook: Once you’ve received your new Enhanced DBS, it’s essential that you register it on the DBS Update Service.

At HCC-Temps, we want to make sure all of our workers understand how this works – and why it matters so much for your career in care.

What is the DBS Update Service?

The DBS Update Service is an online subscription service provided directly by the DBS. Once you’ve applied for a new Enhanced DBS check and received your certificate, you can register it on the service.

This means employers (like us at HCC Temps, and any future care providers you may work with) can carry out quick, secure online checks to see if your DBS status has changed.

You can register your certificate here: DBS Update Service Application

Why Should You Register?

  • Flexibility across roles and employers – If your certificate is on the Update Service, you don’t need to apply for a new DBS every time you start a new placement. Instead, we can simply check the status online.
  • Save time and money – Without the Update Service, every organisation must request a new certificate, even if you already have one in date. That means paying again and waiting for the process to complete.
  • Proof of safeguarding compliance – In health and social care, it’s vital that safeguarding checks are up to date. The Update Service provides peace of mind to both you and the employer that everything is valid and current.

Timeframes You Need to Know

Here’s the catch:

  • You have 30 calendar days from the issue date of your DBS certificate to register it on the Update Service.
  • After those 30 days, you cannot register that certificate. You would need to apply for a brand-new DBS if you want to use the service.

Why Can’t I Just Use My DBS Certificate if It’s Still in Date?

This is a common question. Many people assume that because their certificate is less than a year old, they can use it with different employers.

Unfortunately, that’s not the case. A DBS certificate is a snapshot in time – it only shows information up until the day it was issued.

  • If it’s not on the Update Service, other organisations cannot legally rely on it, because there’s no way to check whether new information has been added since the issue date.
  • This is why, at HCC-Temps, we cannot accept DBS certificates that are not linked to the Update Service – even if they are “in date.”

How HCC Temps Supports You

At HCC Temps, we want to make the process as smooth as possible for all our healthcare professionals.

  • When you apply for a new Enhanced DBS through us, we’ll guide you throughthe steps to register it on the Update Service straight away.
  • Our compliance team will remind you of the deadline so you don’t miss the 30-day window.
  • By making sure your DBS is on the Update Service, you’ll be ready for placements faster, and you’ll have the flexibility to take on new roles without delays.

Final Thoughts

Registering your Enhanced DBS on the Update Service isn’t just a box-ticking exercise – it’s a safeguard that protects you, your employer, and most importantly, the people you care for.

If you’re applying to join HCC Temps, make sure you act quickly once you receive your DBS certificate. Register it on the Update Service within 30 days, and you’ll save yourself time, money, and hassle in the future.

Click here to register your DBS certificate on the Update Service.

Need help? Our compliance team is always here to guide you through the process – so you can focus on what matters most: delivering outstanding care.

title: Agency Chefs for Care Homes in London
excerpt: A day in the life of an agency chef in a London care home: menus, special diets and why care homes use chef recruitment agencies like HCC-Temps for flexible cover.
content:
A Day in the Life of a Care Home Agency Chef

London care homes rely on talented chefs to ensure residents enjoy nutritious meals every day. Agency chefs for care homes offer a flexible solution for care facilities, bringing culinary expertise to the table. These professionals often come via chef recruitment agencies like ours at HCC-temps and they tend to understand the unique needs of care home catering.

This blog offers a glimpse into a typical day in the life of a care home chef in a London care home. The aim of the blog is to inspire new chefs to try a career working in a care home setting.

I hope to highlight a typical daily routine of a care home chef,  looking at interactions with care home residents and staff, while creating a variety of balanced meals they prepare, usually using fresh ingredients and managing the different levels of care, including special and modified diet requirements.

In a care home a typical day’s menu might start with a cooked breakfast option alongside lighter fare like cereal, fruit, and toast.

Lunch usually offers two choices – perhaps a traditional beef pie with mashed potatoes and vegetables, or a lighter fish dish – followed by dessert. A light supper is served for eveining meals– for example, soup and sandwiches or quiche with salad – plus a simple styled pudding like a fruit crumble.

“Contact our team today if to discuss Chef staffing for your care home”

Morning: Starting the Day with Breakfast and Interaction

A care home chef’s day often begins early, around 7:00 or 8:00 am, as they prepare breakfast for the residents. Many residents look forward to a hot cooked breakfast, so the chef may be frying eggs, grilling bacon, or cooking porridge to kick-start the day.

Alongside hot options, the kitchen typically offers a selection of cereals, toast, yoghurts, and fresh fruit. During breakfast service, the chef and care staff work together to ensure each resident gets their preferred meal.

Around this time early risers will come to the kitchen to grab their seat, this is a great time for the chef to get to know the residents’ personal tastes and dietary needs.

Building these relationships is important – unlike restaurant customers, care home residents are long-term “regulars” whom the chef learns about by name and preference over time. These interactions not only brighten the residents’ morning but also give the chef valuable feedback on menu items and portion sizes.

Lunchtime: Delivering Variety, Nutrition, and Modified Diets

Fast forward to later that morning and the focus shifts from breakfast to the main meal of the day: lunch, which is served around 12:30 pm. The chef offers multiple choices so residents can select what appeals to them – typically a hearty classic (like a stew or roast) and a lighter alternative (such as a fish dish).

One of a care home Chef top priorities is to ensure that each resident gets a daily balanced nutrition, so meals can be tailored to individual residents health needs. For example, a resident with diabetes might receive a sugar-free dessert, while someone with a heart condition gets a low-salt meal.

Modified diets are part of the daily routine – it’s common for the chef to prepare chopped, soft, or pureed versions of the main dishes for residents who have difficulty chewing or swallowing. The chef also works closely with care staff to ensure that each resident is served the correct meal and receives any necessary assistance.

Challenges and Benefits

Challenges: Agency care home chefs must cater to a wide range of dietary needs simultaneously – from diabetic diets to low-sodium or pureed meals.

Benefits: On the other hand, being a care home chef is highly rewarding. Chefs build warm relationships with residents. The work hours are often more sociable (daytime shifts with no late nights) compared to restaurant jobs, which helps with work-life balance.

Serving London Care Homes with Excellence

By partnering with chef recruitment agencies, care homes in London can ensure they have the right culinary talent on hand when needed. Our agencies vet each chefs (with enhanced DBS checks and up-to-date food safety training), and can provide cover at short notice to prevent any disruption in service.

From the morning cup of tea right through to the evening supper, our chefs pour their skill and heart into every dish, balancing nutritional needs with personal preferences to bring comfort and joy to residents. For care home managers in London the benefit of working with a chef recruitment agency provides flexibility and ensures the kitchen consistently delivers high-quality, home-style cooked meals for your residents. It’s a partnership that keeps the residents healthy and happy this is what we call “the recipe for a great care home experience”. 

Why Care Home Managers Choose HCC-Temps

At HCC-Temps, we specialise in supplying agency chefs for care homes across London. Our chefs are not only highly trained and fully compliant but also experienced in preparing balanced meals, supporting modified diets, and working seamlessly with care teams.

We understand the challenges care homes face in maintaining consistent, high-quality catering services – whether it’s last-minute cover, long-term placements, or specialist support. We provide flexible, reliable staffing solutions designed to keep your kitchens running smoothly and your residents happy.

Are you are a care home manager in London looking for dependable, skilled catering staff, contact HCC-Temps today to discuss how we can support your care home with trusted chefs and kitchen staff.

title: Why School Meals Matter: Nutrition, Learning & the Role of Hospitality Agencies
excerpt: Why nutritious school meals matter for children's health, wellbeing and learning, and how skilled temporary kitchen staff help school catering teams keep standards high.
content:
The Importance of School Meals: Nutrition, Wellbeing & the Role of Skilled School Kitchen Teams

School meals are far more than just food served at lunchtime—they are a vital part of a child’s health, wellbeing, learning ability, and social development. Across the UK, countless studies and public sector reports highlight how access to nutritious school meals can boost children’s academic performance, improve concentration, reduce behavioural issues, and support long-term health outcomes. For schools, ensuring that meals are delivered safely and consistently often depends on reliable staffing solutions, including school kitchen assistants, chefs, and support staff supplied by a reputable hospitality agency like HCC-Temps.

In today’s education landscape, high-quality school meals matter more than ever. Here’s why:

School Meals Improve Children’s Nutrition and Health

According to research from the School Meals Coalition and the National Institutes of Health, nutritious school meals play a crucial role in children’s daily nutrient intake. For many pupils—especially those from low-income households—school meals may be the most nutritionally balanced meal of the day.

Evidence shows that high-quality school meals can:

  • Improve fruit and vegetable consumption
  • Reduce intake of processed foods and sugary snacks
  • Promote healthier body weight
  • Support long-term eating habits that reduce the risk of chronic diseases

These findings align with research from the South Tyneside Council outlining the health advantages of school meals, particularly when they follow national school food standards.

Better Nutrition = Better Learning

A child who is hungry cannot learn at their best. Studies demonstrate a clear link between balanced meals and improved classroom performance. When children eat a nutritious school meal:

  • Concentration improves
  • Behaviour becomes calmer
  • Memory and problem-solving skills are enhanced
  • Absenteeism decreases

Schools that provide consistent, nutritious meals often report better academic outcomes and more engaged learners. This highlights why it is essential to have well-trained kitchen assistants, cooks, and catering staff in place—roles many schools now fill through specialised hospitality temp agencies.

School Meals Support Social Development

Mealtimes are also powerful social experiences. Children learn how to share, communicate, try new foods, and develop healthy relationships with eating. Lunchtime routines encourage:

  • Social skills
  • Emotional learning
  • Inclusivity and peer support
  • Independence and confidence

For some pupils, the school dining hall is one of the few structured social environments they experience each day.

This makes the role of school kitchen teams even more important. Friendly, consistent staff help create a warm, welcoming atmosphere that supports children as they grow socially and emotionally.

The Essential Role of School Kitchen Assistants & Why Schools Rely on Hospitality Temps

Running a school kitchen takes skill, speed, and organisation. From preparing fresh meals to managing allergens, supporting special diets, and maintaining food safety standards, school kitchen assistants play a vital role in the daily life of a school.

Many schools now turn to hospitality agencies like HCC-Temps to supply experienced kitchen assistants, cooks, and catering support when needed. Hospitality temps bring several advantages:

  • Consistency: Schools can maintain smooth kitchen operations even with staff shortages.
  • Quality: Temps from a specialist hospitality agency often have experience working in fast-paced environments.
  • Flexibility: Schools can scale staffing to match term-time needs and special events.
  • Compliance: Agencies ensure staff have correct training, background checks, and right-to-work documentation.

This flexible model ensures children receive safe, nutritious meals every day—regardless of unexpected staffing challenges.

Why High-Quality School Meals Should Be a National Priority

The School Meals Coalition describes school meals as one of the most impactful public-sector investments a country can make. Not only do meals support children’s health and learning, but they also strengthen communities, reduce inequality, and provide economic benefits by supporting local food supply chains.

title: How to Become an Agency Nurse in the UK: What You Need Before Your First Shift
excerpt: Thinking about agency nursing? Here is what you need in the UK: an NMC PIN, an enhanced DBS, right to work, training certificates and references, plus how to get started fast.
content:
Agency nursing gives Registered Nurses something permanent roles often can't: control over when and where you work. You can pick up extra shifts around a permanent job, work full time across several care homes, or build a schedule around family life. But before your first agency shift, there are a few things every agency in the UK will need to see.

This guide explains exactly what you need, why each check matters, and how to get through registration quickly.

1. An active NMC PIN

To work as a Registered Nurse (RGN or RMN) in the UK you must be on the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) register. Your PIN shows your registration is active, and agencies check it on the NMC's online register before offering you shifts.

  • Keep your annual fee paid and your revalidation up to date (every three years).
  • Have your NMC Statement of Entry to hand: it confirms your registration details.
  • If you trained overseas, you will need to have completed the NMC's registration process before working as a Registered Nurse.

2. An enhanced DBS on the Update Service

Nursing in care homes and hospitals means working with vulnerable people, so an enhanced DBS check (with barred list checks) is required. If your certificate is on the DBS Update Service, an agency can check it online in minutes instead of waiting weeks for a new one.

You have 30 days from the date your certificate is issued to join the Update Service. We explain why it is worth doing in Have you put your enhanced DBS on the Update Service? No DBS yet? That's fine: register with us and we will apply for one for you.

3. Proof of your right to work

Every UK employer and agency must check your right to work before you start. British and Irish citizens usually show a valid passport. If you hold a visa or settled status, you will share a right to work share code from GOV.UK. Our guide Right to work checks for agency staff explains how share codes work.

4. Up-to-date training certificates

Care settings expect nurses to hold current mandatory training. The usual list includes Basic Life Support, Manual Handling, Safeguarding Adults and Children, Infection Prevention and Control, Fire Safety, Health and Safety, Information Governance, Mental Capacity Act and DoLS, Medication Administration, and the Oliver McGowan training on learning disability and autism.

Missing a course? You can buy and complete courses online through our e-learning portal, then upload the certificates in your candidate portal. See Mandatory training for care workers for the full list.

5. Your documents and references

Expect to provide:

  • An up-to-date CV covering the last few years of work, with any gaps explained
  • Photo ID (passport or driving licence)
  • Two proofs of address from the last three months (two different documents)
  • Proof of your National Insurance number
  • A professional photo for your ID badge
  • Your nursing diploma or degree, and immunisation records where applicable
  • Details of two professional referees, ideally recent managers

What agency nursing is like day to day

Most agency nurses work in nursing homes, residential homes with nursing, and hospitals. You will often be the nurse in charge of a unit, so confidence with medication rounds, care plans, clinical observations such as NEWS2 and handovers is essential. Good agencies send you back to the same homes where possible, so you get to know the residents and the team.

Flexibility works both ways: you choose the shifts that suit you, and homes rely on you to arrive on time, follow their procedures and communicate clearly. Reliability is what turns a first shift into regular work.

How to get started with HCC-Temps

Registration happens online, step by step, and most candidates are ready to work within 3 days:

  1. Choose Registered Nurse and create your account.
  2. Answer a few questions about your right to work, DBS and experience.
  3. Upload your documents and training certificates from your phone. Anything you don't have yet can follow later.
  4. Our compliance team checks everything and keeps you updated in your portal.

You can also browse current nursing jobs or call us any time on 0330 321 3124.

Frequently asked questions

Can I work agency shifts alongside a permanent nursing job?

Yes. Many of our nurses do. Check your permanent contract for any restrictions, and make sure you get enough rest between shifts.

Do I need a new DBS for every agency?

Not if your enhanced DBS is on the Update Service and covers the right workforce. The agency can check its status online with your permission.

How quickly can I start?

If your documents and training are ready, most candidates are cleared within 3 days of registering.

title: Agency Healthcare Assistant Jobs: Documents, Training and Your First Shift
excerpt: Want flexible healthcare assistant shifts in care homes? Find out which documents, checks and training you need, what to expect on your first shift and how to register quickly.
content:
Healthcare assistants (HCAs) and care assistants are the heart of every care home. Agency work lets you choose your shifts, try different settings and build experience quickly, whether you are new to care or have years behind you. Here is what you need to get started.

Who can become an agency healthcare assistant?

You don't always need formal qualifications to start, but care homes look for people who are kind, reliable and confident with personal care. Experience in a care home, hospital, home care or supported living is a big advantage. Qualifications such as the Care Certificate or a Level 2 or 3 Diploma in Health and Social Care show you know the standards expected.

The checks every agency will make

Enhanced DBS

Because you will be supporting vulnerable adults, you need an enhanced DBS check with barred list checks. If your certificate is on the DBS Update Service, it can be checked online straight away. If you don't have one, we can apply for one for you.

Right to work

Your passport, or a share code if you hold a visa or settled status. See how right to work checks work.

References

Two professional referees, ideally your most recent managers. We contact them for you.

Documents to have ready

  • CV with your recent work history
  • Passport or driving licence
  • Two proofs of address from the last three months (two different documents)
  • Proof of National Insurance number
  • A head-and-shoulders photo for your ID badge

Clear photos taken on your phone are fine: lay each document flat in daylight with all four corners showing.

Training you will need

Care homes expect HCAs to hold current certificates in the core subjects: Basic Life Support, Manual Handling (theory and practical), Safeguarding Adults and Children, Infection Prevention and Control, Health and Safety, Fire Safety, Food Safety, First Aid, Equality and Diversity, Information Governance, and Mental Capacity Act and DoLS. Senior carers usually also need Medication Administration.

If some are missing or out of date, you can buy and complete the courses online through our e-learning portal. The full list is in Mandatory training for care workers.

What to expect on your first shift

  • Arrive 10 to 15 minutes early and sign in with the nurse or senior in charge.

title: Dementia Care Homes with Specialised Nutrition Programs in the UK: Why Expert Chefs Make the Difference
excerpt: How specialised nutrition programmes support residents in UK dementia care homes, and why experienced chefs who understand texture-modified and fortified diets make the difference.
content:
Dementia care homes with specialised nutrition programs in the UK (and how to staff them well)

In UK dementia care homes, nutrition is never “just the food.” It’s hydration, dignity, routine, safety, and one of the most reliable ways to improve day-to-day wellbeing. As the Royal College of Nursing puts it, “Mealtimes are fundamental to health and quality of life.” (The Royal College of Nursing)

That’s why more dementia care homes are building specialised nutrition programs—not “special diets,” but practical, person-centred systems that help residents eat and drink well even as needs change. And crucially, these programs only work when the kitchen is staffed by chefs and kitchen teams who understand dementia-friendly catering.

If you’re a care provider looking for a chef (or a full kitchen team) with dementia experience, HCC-Temps Staffing Agency supports UK care homes with reliable, trained catering staff. You’ll find more details at hcctemps.co.uk.

What “specialised nutrition” really means in dementia care homes

The Alzheimer’s Society notes that “People with dementia often experience problems with eating and drinking.” (Alzheimer’s Society) Those problems can include reduced appetite, forgetfulness, sensory changes, difficulty using cutlery, or swallowing issues (dysphagia). So the best dementia nutrition programs focus on supporting eating, rather than restricting it.

 

The British Dietetic Association (BDA) warns against overly strict food rules: “It is crucial to avoid restrictive diets for patients with dementia.” (British Dietetic Association) In practice, that often means prioritising enjoyment and intake—while still managing clinical risks with professional guidance.

The core building blocks of a strong dementia nutrition program

Here’s what high-performing dementia care homes in the UK commonly build into their nutrition and hydration approach.

1) Nutrition screening + clear care plans

Malnutrition risk is common in older adults. Age UK estimates “around one in ten” over-65s are malnourished or at risk in the UK. (Age UK)

Many care homes use BAPEN’s ‘MUST’ screening process—“a five-step screening tool to identify adults… malnourished [or] at risk of malnutrition.” (BAPEN) Screening is only useful if it leads to action, and NICE is explicit that people at risk should have a plan: “All people… at risk of malnutrition should receive a nutritional care plan.” (Clinical Knowledge Summaries)

Kitchen impact: chefs need to be able to follow nutrition care plans consistently—especially when intake dips or weight changes.

2) Dementia-friendly dining that increases intake

The RCN highlights how powerful good mealtime support can be: “Good mealtime care is transformational to the experience of people with dementia living in care homes.” (The Royal College of Nursing)

Common features include:

  • Finger foods and “little-and-often” menus for people who wander or struggle to sit through meals
  • High-contrast plates and simplified table settings (to reduce confusion)
  • Familiar foods and culturally appropriate menus (comfort drives intake)
  • Flexible meal times (when appetite is best, not when the rota says so)

Kitchen impact: dementia care homes benefit from chefs who can cook home-style, adapt presentation, and work closely with care staff.

3) Fortified foods and “food-first” energy/protein strategies

When appetite is low, portion size often needs to go down—but nutrition must go up. Many specialist programs rely on:

  • Fortified mash/soups/sauces
  • High-protein snacks and puddings
  • Nourishing drinks between meals

Kitchen impact: this is where skilled care-home chefs shine—because fortification must still taste good, look appealing, and fit individual preferences.

4) Hydration that’s actively supported (not passively offered)

Dehydration risk rises with memory issues and reduced thirst cues. The RCN advises: “Encourage people to drink small amounts throughout the day.” (The Royal College of Nursing)

Specialised hydration programs often include:

  • Drink rounds with choice and prompts
  • Jelly/ice-lollies/fruit options for people who reject cups
  • Hydration support at medication times

Kitchen impact: kitchens often own the beverage offer. A well-run kitchen can make hydration effortless, appealing, and routine.

5) Texture-modified diets and dysphagia safety

Swallowing difficulties need specialist input. NICE states people with indicators of dysphagia “should be referred to… specialist training… for example speech and language therapists.” (NICE)

Many care homes align with speech and language therapy guidance and structured texture frameworks, then translate that into:

  • Consistent texture-modified meals
  • Safer thickened fluids where prescribed
  • Clear kitchen labelling and cross-checks

Kitchen impact: texture modification is a skill. The right chef prevents risk while keeping meals enjoyable.

What care providers should look for when hiring a dementia care chef

If you’re recruiting for a dementia care home kitchen, use this quick checklist to find people who can deliver a specialist nutrition program—not just cook a menu.

Your dementia-friendly chef should be able to:

  • Cook appetising soft/texture-modified meals without “puree plate boredom”
  • Fortify meals to increase calories/protein without huge portions
  • Work to nutrition care plans and respond quickly to intake changes
  • Support finger foods, snack programs, and flexible meal services
  • Communicate calmly with residents and collaborate with care staff

This is exactly where specialist staffing support helps.

How HCC-Temps Staffing Agency supports dementia care homes

Specialised nutrition programs succeed when the kitchen is stable, covered, and led by people who understand care environments. HCC-Temps Staffing Agency helps UK care homes source dependable chefs and kitchen staff—particularly where dementia-friendly catering, consistency, and compliance matter.

If your service is:

  • Expanding dementia beds
  • Upgrading to a more structured nutrition/hydration program
  • Struggling with chef shortages, sickness cover, or last-minute cancellations
  • Needing cooks confident with fortified meals and texture-modified diets

…then it’s worth speaking with a staffing partner who understands the pace and expectations of care catering.

To hire a dementia-experienced chef or kitchen team, visit hcctemps.co.uk and connect with HCC-Temps Staffing Agency.

Final thought: the best dementia nutrition programs are human programs

Guidance, screening tools, and care plans matter—but residents experience food emotionally: comfort, identity, and routine. When a care home invests in dementia-friendly dining and hires chefs who can deliver it consistently, nutrition becomes one of the strongest daily supports you can provide.

title: Right to Work Checks for Agency Staff: Share Codes Explained
excerpt: Every agency must check your right to work in the UK before your first shift. Here is how share codes, passports and eVisas work, and how to avoid delays when you register.
content:
Before anyone can start work in the UK, the employer or agency must check they have the right to work here. It is a legal requirement, and agencies can face heavy penalties for getting it wrong. The good news is that for most people the check takes minutes, as long as you have the right document or code ready.

British and Irish citizens

If you are a British or Irish citizen, you usually prove your right to work with a valid passport (an Irish passport card is also accepted). Some employers use an approved digital identity service to check passports online.

If you don't have a valid passport, other documents may be accepted, such as a full birth or adoption certificate together with an official document showing your National Insurance number. Ask us if you're unsure.

Everyone else: the share code

If you have a visa, settled or pre-settled status under the EU Settlement Scheme, or another immigration status, your right to work is held digitally. You prove it with a share code.

  1. Go to the GOV.UK service Prove your right to work to an employer.
  2. Sign in with your UKVI account details.
  3. Choose to share your right to work. You will get a share code that starts with W.
  4. Give us the share code and your date of birth. We check it on GOV.UK.

A share code is valid for 90 days. If yours has expired, simply create a new one.

eVisas have replaced BRP cards

Physical biometric residence permits (BRPs) have been replaced by eVisas, an online record of your immigration status. If you haven't set up your UKVI account yet, do this first: you need it to create a share code.

Visa conditions matter

Some visas come with conditions that affect the work you can do:

  • Student visas usually limit the hours you can work during term time. Agencies will ask for your university's term dates.
  • Health and Care Worker and Skilled Worker visas are tied to a sponsoring employer, and other work may be restricted. Your certificate of sponsorship shows the details.
  • Dependant and family visas vary: the share code result shows any restrictions.

Being honest about your visa type when you register helps us find shifts that fit your conditions.

How HCC-Temps checks your right to work

When you register with us, we ask whether you are a British or Irish citizen. If you are, your passport upload covers the check. If not, we ask for your visa type and share code, and our compliance team checks it on GOV.UK and records the result, including any visa expiry date, so we can remind you before it runs out.

For care home managers

When you book agency staff, the agency carries out the right to work checks and keeps the records. Choosing an agency with a clear compliance process protects your home. At HCC-Temps every candidate's checks are recorded, with who checked and when, before they are offered shifts. See how we supply staff.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a share code last?

90 days from when it was created. You can create a new one at any time.

Can I start work while my visa application is being processed?

It depends on your circumstances. The employer may need to use the Home Office's Employer Checking Service. Contact us and we will advise.

I'm a British citizen without a passport. What can I use?

A full birth certificate with an official document showing your National Insurance number is one accepted combination. We will guide you.

title: Mandatory Training for Care Workers: The Courses You Need and How to Get Them Online
excerpt: The mandatory training care workers, healthcare assistants and nurses need in the UK, how often to refresh it, and how to buy courses online through the HCC-Temps e-learning portal.
content:
Whether you are a healthcare assistant, senior carer or Registered Nurse, care homes expect you to hold up-to-date training certificates before you start. Training keeps residents safe, protects you, and shows the home you know the standards. Here are the courses you will need and how to get them quickly.

The core courses for care roles

  • Basic Life Support: what to do in a cardiac or breathing emergency.
  • Manual Handling: moving and positioning people safely. Care homes often ask for theory and practical.
  • Safeguarding Adults and Safeguarding Children: recognising and reporting abuse and neglect.
  • Infection Prevention and Control: hand hygiene, PPE and stopping the spread of infection.
  • Health and Safety: risk assessment and safe working.
  • Fire Safety: prevention, alarms and evacuation.
  • Food Safety: safe food handling when helping with meals.
  • First Aid: responding to injuries until help arrives.
  • Equality and Diversity: person-centred, respectful care.
  • Information Governance / GDPR: keeping personal information confidential.
  • Mental Capacity Act and DoLS: consent, capacity and deprivation of liberty safeguards.

Extra training for some roles

  • Medication Administration for nurses and senior carers who give medicines.
  • Autism and Learning Disability awareness, including the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training, now expected across health and social care.
  • Clinical skills such as observations and NEWS2 for nursing teams.

How often do you need to refresh training?

Most care homes expect mandatory training to be refreshed regularly, often every year for subjects like Basic Life Support, Manual Handling, Infection Control and Fire Safety. Others may be every two or three years. When you register, upload your certificates and add the expiry dates, so you know when each one is due.

Certificates must show your full name and the date you completed the course.

Buy your training online with HCC-Temps

If you are missing a course or one has expired, you don't need to wait for a classroom date. Through the HCC-Temps e-learning portal, delivered with our partner VideoTile Learning, you can buy courses and complete them online at your own pace, on your phone or computer.

  1. Visit the e-learning portal from your candidate portal, or ask us for the link.
  2. Buy the courses you need. Prices are shown before you pay, and there is a free trial.
  3. Complete the course and download your certificate.
  4. Upload the certificate in your HCC-Temps portal under Training. Our compliance team checks it.

Prefer help choosing? Message the team from your portal and we will tell you exactly which courses you still need.

Training for chefs and kitchen staff

Kitchen roles have their own list, usually Food Safety and Hygiene (Level 2, or Level 3 for chefs who supervise), Allergen Awareness, Health and Safety and First Aid. See our guide to agency chef work in care homes.

Ready to register?

Choose your role to see exactly which documents and training it needs. You can register even if some training is missing: we will help you get it sorted.

Frequently asked questions

Is online training accepted by care homes?

Accredited online courses are widely accepted for theory subjects. Some homes also ask for practical sessions, for example manual handling.

Can I register before my training is complete?

Yes. Upload what you have and tick "I don't have this yet" for the rest. We will remind you what is outstanding.

What if my certificate has expired?

You will need to refresh it before working. Online courses are usually the quickest way.

title: Agency Chef Work in Care Homes: Food Hygiene, Allergens and Texture-Modified Diets
excerpt: What it takes to be an agency chef in a care home: food hygiene certificates, allergen rules, IDDSI texture-modified diets, fortified meals, and how to register with HCC-Temps.
content:
Cooking for a care home is different from restaurant work. Your diners might be 95, living with dementia, or need every meal pureed. Mealtimes are a highlight of the day, and good food directly supports residents' health, hydration and dignity. Agency chefs who understand this are in real demand.

Qualifications care homes look for

  • Food Safety and Hygiene, Level 2 as a minimum, and Level 3 if you run or supervise the kitchen. Certificates should be in date.
  • Allergen Awareness, Level 3 for chefs who plan menus.
  • Health and Safety and First Aid.
  • An enhanced DBS, as you work in a care setting with vulnerable adults.

Missing a certificate? You can buy courses online through our e-learning portal. See our training guide.

Allergens: the 14 you must know

UK law requires food businesses, including care home kitchens, to manage and communicate the 14 major allergens: celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, tree nuts, peanuts, sesame, soya, and sulphur dioxide and sulphites. Keep allergen records up to date for every dish, check each resident's dietary sheet, and never substitute ingredients without updating the records.

Texture-modified diets and IDDSI

Many residents have dysphagia (difficulty swallowing). Their speech and language therapist sets the texture they need using the IDDSI framework, levels 0 to 7 for drinks and foods, from thin liquids to regular food. As a care home chef you may prepare:

  • Level 4, pureed: smooth, no lumps, holds its shape on a spoon.
  • Level 5, minced and moist: small soft lumps, easy to mash.
  • Level 6, soft and bite-sized: tender pieces no bigger than 1.5cm.

Getting the texture wrong is a choking risk, so always follow the resident's plan, use the IDDSI testing methods (such as the fork pressure test), and present texture-modified meals attractively. Moulded purees that look like the original dish make a real difference to appetite. Read more in why expert chefs make the difference in dementia care.

Fortified food and hydration

Older people are at risk of malnutrition and dehydration. Chefs help by fortifying meals (adding butter, cream, cheese or milk powder for extra calories and protein), offering snacks between meals, and making drinks appealing. CQC's regulations require homes to meet residents' nutrition and hydration needs, and the kitchen is central to that.

Kitchen safety and COSHH

Cleaning chemicals must be stored, used and recorded safely. See our guide to COSHH in care home kitchens. Keep temperature records for fridges, freezers, cooking and hot holding.

What a typical agency chef shift looks like

  • Arrive early, meet the manager or senior, check the menu and dietary sheets.
  • Prepare breakfast, lunch and tea from set menus, plus texture-modified and special diets.
  • Complete allergen, temperature and cleaning records.
  • Leave the kitchen clean, stock rotated, and a clear handover for the next cook.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need care home experience to be a care home chef?

It helps, but strong food hygiene, allergen knowledge and a willingness to learn texture-modified diets are what homes look for most.

Which food hygiene level do I need?

Level 2 as a minimum. Head chefs and anyone supervising usually need Level 3.

Can I work in schools as well as care homes?

Yes. We also cover school kitchens. Read why school meals matter.

title: Temporary vs Permanent Staff in Care Homes: Costs, Flexibility and Continuity of Care
excerpt: Should your care home rely on permanent staff, agency staff or a mix? A practical look at costs, flexibility, continuity of care and compliance, and how to use agency staff well.
content:
Most care homes need both permanent staff and agency support. Getting the balance right affects your budget, your CQC rating and, most importantly, the experience of the people who live in your home. Here's a practical way to think about it.

The case for a strong permanent team

  • Continuity of care: residents know the faces, and staff know residents' routines, preferences and early signs of illness.
  • Culture: a stable team shares your values and standards.
  • Lower hourly cost for regular hours you can predict.

But permanent staffing alone rarely covers everything. Sickness, holidays, training days, vacancies and rising dependency all create gaps.

Where agency staff add value

  • Short-notice cover for sickness and emergencies, often within hours. See how emergency cover works.
  • Flexibility during recruitment gaps, winter pressure, outbreaks or when a resident needs one-to-one support.
  • No recruitment or onboarding cost for the shifts you book: vetting, checks and training records are handled by the agency.
  • Specialist skills on demand, such as nurses or experienced chefs for texture-modified diets.

Understanding the real cost

Agency hourly rates are higher than permanent pay rates, because they include the agency's costs: employer National Insurance, holiday pay, pension contributions, compliance checks and 24-hour support. When comparing, look at the full cost of a permanent employee too: recruitment, induction, training, sick pay, holiday cover and management time. For unpredictable or short-term needs, agency cover is often the more economical choice.

The Agency Workers Regulations

Under the Agency Workers Regulations 2010, agency workers who stay in the same role with the same hirer for 12 weeks become entitled to the same basic working and employment conditions as if they had been recruited directly, including pay. From day one they also have access to facilities such as staff rooms and information about vacancies. Your agency should manage this with you.

How to get the best from agency staff

  1. Ask for regular faces. A good agency builds a small pool of workers who know your home.
  2. Book ahead where you can. Planned shifts give the agency time to send your preferred staff.
  3. Use a short agency induction covering fire safety, emergencies, care plans and who to ask.
  4. Give feedback: good and bad. It shapes who is sent next time.
  5. Check compliance. You should be able to see evidence of each worker's DBS, right to work, references and training.

A blended approach works best

The strongest homes build a stable permanent core and use a trusted agency for the rest: the same familiar agency workers on planned shifts, plus fast cover in emergencies. That protects continuity of care while keeping staffing safe and costs under control.

Yes. Tell us who works well with your residents and we will prioritise them.
